analysis.one_liner: Bans partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts and lets voters sue to overturn rigged maps.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar states from drawing congressional district lines with the purpose or effect of unduly favoring one political party. It would let any eligible voter sue in federal court to strike down a gerrymandered map, require courts to appoint special masters to draw remedial maps when a state is found in violation, ban mid-decade redistricting after a remedial plan, and require states to publish their map data and hold public hearings before voting on a plan. It never moved beyond being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters in states where congressional maps are drawn to lock in one party's advantage. Fairer maps would mean more competitive elections, representatives who must answer to a broader range of voters, and a public process with published map data, hearings, and written justifications before any plan is adopted.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any state congressional districting plan that has the purpose or effect of unduly favoring or disfavoring a political party [S2][S3].
Gives any eligible voter the right to sue in federal court to invalidate a partisan map, and bars legislators from hiding behind legislative privilege in such cases [S3].

Requires states to consider communities of interest and equal opportunity for racial and language minority voters, and forbids map drawers from using party registration, voting history, precinct election results, or incumbents' home addresses [S3].
Creates a safe harbor for maps drawn by bipartisan or nonpartisan redistricting commissions, which get a rebuttable presumption of validity [S3].

Requires public hearings with at least 10 days' notice, publication of the demographic data and map files used to draw plans, and a written report 72 hours before any vote explaining how a plan satisfies fairness measures [S3].

Bars a state from redrawing its congressional map again before the next census once a court-approved remedial plan is in place, unless a court requires it to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislators and party operatives who currently draw maps to protect their seats. They would lose the ability to choose their voters, would have to justify maps in public with published data, and could see their maps struck down by lawsuits filed by any voter in the state.

drawbacks.text: The bill substitutes courts and court-appointed special masters for elected legislatures when a map is struck down, and the standard 'unduly favors or disfavors a political party' is open-ended, so enforcement would depend heavily on judicial interpretation and statistical measures of partisan fairness that experts themselves contest [S3].

Litigation by any single eligible voter could keep a state's maps tied up in federal court, and the bill forbids courts from staying remedial map-drawing while an appeal is pending, which could produce maps imposed quickly before appeals are resolved [S3].
The bill as introduced applied only to congressional districts, not to state legislative districts, so gerrymandered statehouse maps would remain untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: voters choosing their representatives instead of representatives choosing their voters, with a workable enforcement mechanism modeled on three-judge courts already used in redistricting cases. The costs are procedural rather than substantive: more litigation, judicial involvement in drawing maps, and a fairness standard that courts would have to define over time. The main weakness is not design but reach — it covers congressional maps only, leaving most gerrymandering of state legislatures in place. On balance, an honest supporter would acknowledge the vagueness and litigation risk while arguing that the status quo the bill targets is itself far worse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never considered it; it died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the Fair Maps Act of 2019 on June 25, 2019 [S1][S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor [S4].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction, and the action history records no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee without a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the legislators who draw congressional maps are better off, because nothing disturbed their ability to draw districts that protect their seats.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Maps Act of 2019 and spoke for it by sponsoring it; it was his bill alone.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the committee held no action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measure of broader support in either party.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators who draw maps
industries.note: Gerrymandering lets map-drawers choose their voters, and the bill would ban the practice for congressional maps, expose the data behind maps, and open incumbents' maps to voter lawsuits. Its defeat preserves their control over district lines.

Both major parties gain safe seats where they control map-drawing, and the bill would prohibit using party registration, voting history, and precinct results to draw congressional districts. Its death leaves that tool intact.

industries.industry: Political map-drawing consultants and data firms
industries.note: Partisan map-drawing is a professional industry that sells sophistication in building districts with the help of voter files and election data. Because the bill never became law, states can keep hiring private consultants to draw maps outside public view.
